To launch RStudio server, first start an interactive session in SEDNA. You won’t need much computing resources, since MitoPilot uses Nextflow to distribute the analyses.

srun -c 2 --mem=16GB -p standard --pty /bin/bash

Then run the following.

mamba activate MitoPilot_deps
start-rstudio-server-MitoPilot

Follow the instructions to access your RStudio server session. They should look something like this.
TO ACCESS RSTUDIO SERVER
In a terminal on your local system, run the following command:
ssh -N -L 8787:node01.cluster:8377 dmacguigan@sedna.nwfsc2.noaa.gov

Enter your password when prompted
If successful, nothing will happen
Then open http://localhost:8787 on a local web browser

NOTE: This window and your local terminal session
must remain open in order to access the Rstudio server



Once you have opened the RStudio server session, run library(MitoPilot) to load the package. You should see a message about Nextflow if successful.
Want to learn how to use MitoPilot? Check out the MitoPilot workshop website.



On SEDNA, run the pipeline as a batch job rather than in an interactive session. An interactive run needs you to hold the connection open for the whole workflow, which is fine for a handful of samples and risky for a few dozen or more.
MitoPilot builds the submission script for you. Click Update, and the update window shows a ready-to-edit SLURM script pre-filled with #SBATCH directives. Add the SEDNA environment setup where the script indicates:

source ~/.bashrc
mamba activate MitoPilot_deps

Then use “Save Script Only” and submit the written .sh from a normal shell with sbatch. Do not use “Submit to Cluster” if you launched the app from a container, because sbatch is not available inside it. Your edits to the resource block are remembered per project, so the next run pre-fills them.
Monitor the job with squeue and the log files. When it finishes, relaunch the GUI to inspect the results. The same approach works for the annotate module. See Running the pipeline in the Custom HPC vignette for the full description of the submission window.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
This page is for projects where you already have both a mitogenome assembly and an annotation for every sample. Initialize such a project with new_project_userAnnot(). MitoPilot will import your assembly and features, ask you to confirm the gene names, then curates validate, and export the annotations them like any other project.
Read Starting Your Own Project and Using Your Own Assemblies first. This page covers only what differs.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
Setting up the project
The mapping file takes the user-assembly columns (Assembly and Topology) plus one more (Annotation):







Column
Contents




Assembly
File name of the assembly FASTA for the sample. Exactly one sequence per file.


Topology
Optional. circular or linear. Any sample with this unspecified defaults to linear.


Annotation
File name of the annotation for the sample: GFF3 (.gff, .gff3), BED (.bed), or a GenBank 5-column feature table (.tbl).



The sequence ID inside each annotation must equal the first word of the FASTA header. For an assembly whose FASTA header is >NC_002333 Danio rerio mitochondrion, the ID is NC_002333 and each format carries it like so:
GFF3, first column of every feature line:
##gff-version 3
NC_002333   RefSeq  gene    951 1019    .   +   .   ID=gene-trnF;Name=trnF
NC_002333   RefSeq  tRNA    951 1019    .   +   .   ID=rna-trnF;Parent=gene-trnF;product=tRNA-Phe
BED, first column of every line:
NC_002333   950 1019    tRNA-Phe    0   +
NC_002333   1019    1971    12S rRNA    0   +
GenBank feature table, the >Feature line at the top of the file:
>Feature NC_002333
951 1019    gene
            gene    trnF
951 1019    tRNA
            product tRNA-Phe
Copies of your original files are kept in <project>/user_annotations/raw/.
new_project_userAnnot(
  path = "~/my_annotated/run_01",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_annotated/mapping.csv",
  assembly_path = "~/my_annotated/fasta",
  annotation_path = "~/my_annotated/annotations",
  no_raw_data = TRUE
)
Reads are optional. With data_path and R1/R2 columns, the Assemble module maps them to calculate coverage. Specify no_raw_data = TRUE if you do not have sequence reads for your samples.
Mitogenome identification, circularization, and scaffold joining are not available for this project type, since any of them would shift the coordinates of your annotation. Coverage trimming and start-gene rotation are off by default for the same reason.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
What MitoPilot imports
Aside from the gene name and coordinates, MitoPilot will also attempt to import the following information.

Partial ends, reading frame (codon_start), and anticodons.
Pseudogenes, with the note import: pseudogene.
Free-text notes, as import: <note>. They are shown in the details window but not written on export.
Introns and ribosomal slippage, as MitoPilot join groups. The feature-table export writes the ribosomal_slippage and exception qualifiers back.

transl_except is not stored. MitoPilot derives it from the shortened stop codon the coordinates give, and export regenerates it.
Every other attribute or qualifier (e.g. locus_tag, db_xref, gbkey) is stored verbatim in project database table user_annotations. MitoPilot does not display or export these, they are kept only for reference.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
Reviewing gene names
MitoPilot guesses a canonical gene name for every feature when the project is created. The first time you open the app, the Imported gene names window lists every name from your annotation files with its guess.

Fix any wrong guesses with the picker in the gene column or select (drop) for any features you do not wish to include. Expand a row to see which samples and features carry that name. Rows you edit count as Edited and leave the Unmapped view. When you are finished, press Confirm.
Pipeline runs are blocked until you confirm. The app header shows a notice with a Review button until then. Use the Gene names toolbar button to reopen this window at any time. Confirming a second time re-queues only the samples whose gene names actually changed.
Names MitoPilot cannot place, such as ORFs or the light-strand origin (OL). Control-region names (D-loop, control region, OH) import as MitoPilot’s control region feature, ctrl, which exports as D-loop.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
Running the pipeline
Once the names are confirmed, start by running Update in the Assemble module. This will only BLAST your mitogenomes and map sequence reads (if available). Then lock the samples and run Update in the Annotate module.
By default, the Annotate workflow does not run any annotation tool. It simply curates and validates your imported annotations.

After running the Annotate workflow, open the details window for each sample. Notes that start with import: were carried over from your file. Any changes made by MitoPilot curation will also be recorded in the Notes column.

The Sequence and BLAST Reference Synteny viewers in that window draw your original annotation as a muted track above the curated one, labelled with the gene names from your file. A feature outlined in amber is one MitoPilot changed: its coordinates or strand moved, curation dropped it, or its name was never mapped. Hover an arrow for the reason and the coordinates as they appear in your file. A name change alone (COI becoming cox1) is not marked. The track follows the Linearize and Trim buttons; a feature a trim cuts through is drawn clipped and marked as such. Untick “Original” in either viewer to hide it.
When done reviewing, you may continue with Export as usual.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
Filling gaps with MitoPilot’s tools
By default MitoPilot annotates nothing when you provide the annotations. However, if your annotations are incomplete, MitoPilot’s own tools can help fill the gaps.
In the Annotate options window, tick Run annotation tools. When it is on, the tools chosen in the Tools box run on each assembly. If these tools identify a missing annotation, they add it to your sample.

Your annotations always win. A feature identified by MitoPilot is dropped when it overlaps one of your annotations with the same gene name, or when more than 10% of its length overlaps any of your features.
The Annotate table has a Found by MitoPilot column that reports the number of features added per sample. Hover over the number to see additional details.

In the details window of the Annotate module, the “Tool” columns lists the source of each feature.
For example, in the test project, the annotation for sample GB_GAPS is deliberately missing cox2, nad3, trnD, trnK, and rrnS. If you run this sample with MitoPilot annotation enabled, you should see all of the missing features are added back.

title: Using Your Own Annotations
text:
Test project details
new_test_project_userAnnot() creates seven samples, each a RefSeq fish mitogenome with small simulated reads:







Sample
Annotation




GB_NCBI
NCBI GFF3 with the full gene/mRNA/CDS/exon hierarchy


GB_TBL
NCBI feature table with anticodons


GB_BED
BED, with one gene split into two blocks


GB_TYPOS
GFF3 with odd and misspelled gene names; several are left for you to map


GB_DROP
Feature table with features that are dropped or flagged on import: gaps, a pseudogene, ribosomal slippage, partial ends, a gene spanning the origin, and two control-region features


GB_MITOS
MITOS2-style GFF with lowercase names and numbered tRNAs


GB_GAPS
GFF3 missing five genes (cox2, nad3, trnD, trnK, rrnS); turn on Run annotation tools to see MitoPilot fill them in

title: Difficult Annotations
text:
The default annotation settings work well for most vertebrates. For other clades, annotations may be missing genes, have genes on the wrong strand, or gene boundaries that do not match the references. This page provides some troubleshooting tips.
Work in this order:
All settings below can be found in the options windows of the Annotate module: select the problematic assemblies, click the Annotation, Curation, or ORF finder options cell, and tick Edit. Saving sets the selected assemblies to state Ready to run; press Update to annotate them again.

title: Difficult Annotations
text:
A gene is missing

Try a different MITOS2 reference database
MITOS2 is the main annotator. It finds genes by comparing your assembly to a set of reference mitogenomes, chosen with MITOS2 reference database: Chordata or Metazoa_RefSeq89. For anything that is not a chordate, switch to Metazoa_RefSeq89. This is sometimes the only change needed.


Check the two MITOS2 switches

Keep only best of overlapping predictions (–best). On by default. When MITOS2 predicts two overlapping features, only the top-scoring one is kept. If a real gene overlaps a stronger prediction, turning this off can bring it back, at the cost of more duplicates that you have to manually delete.
Rescue rRNAs/PCGs lost to tRNA overlap. On by default. MITOS2 runs a second time without tRNA prediction, to recover rRNAs and protein-coding genes it drops when a tRNA overlaps them. Leave it on unless you need the shorter run time.



Add more annotation tools
Three more annotation tools can run alongside the defaults. Each one only fills gaps: when tools disagree, the higher-priority tool wins:

Genes and rRNAs: MITOS2 > MitoFinder.
tRNAs: tRNAscan-SE > ARWEN > ARAGORN > MITOS2.

Also use MitoFinder for annotation. MitoFinder finds genes by similarity to a GenBank-format reference file that you supply in MitoFinder reference database (.gb format). It helps most when you have good annotated mitogenomes from close relatives. Build the reference database with custom_assembly_db(); see building custom databases. Two extra checkboxes appear: Annotate non-standard genes (–new-genes) and Search for genes with introns (–allow-intron).
Also use ARWEN/ARAGORN for tRNA prediction. Both are tRNA finders that catch unusual tRNAs, such as those with a missing arm. Turn on one or both when tRNAs are absent. Each has its own options box, with a “?” that shows the tool’s command-line options for more control.


Adjust tRNAscan-SE for your clade
The default tRNAscan-SE options are -M vert -X 20. -M vert is the vertebrate mitochondrial model; tRNAscan-SE has mitochondrial models only for vertebrates and mammals. In practice, we have found that the vertebrate model performs well for many invertebrate mitogenomes. But if your annotation is missing tRNAs, you could try replacing -M vert with -O (other organellar tRNAs). -X is the score cut-off; lowering it reports weaker tRNAs. The “?” beside the options box shows every flag.
If a tRNA is found but its anticodon could not be determined, it is dropped by default. Tick Retain low-confidence (NNN anticodon) tRNAs to keep these, then check each one by hand.


Keep the ends of linear assemblies
Trim un-annotated ends of linear contigs (by gene features) removes base pairs beyond the outermost annotated gene. If a gene near the end was missed, the trim removes the sequence it sits on. Turn this off before trying the ORF finder or Liftover on a linear assembly.


Look for unannotated open reading frames (ORFs)
For genes that are poorly represented in the reference databases, such as lineage-specific ORFs, open the ORF finder options and tick Run ORF finder step. After curation, NCBI ORFfinder scans for ORFs in regions with no annotation.

Min ORF length (nt) sets the shortest ORF reported.
Max overlap w/ existing annotations sets how much of an ORF may overlap a gene that is already annotated.
Include nested/overlapping ORFs also reports ORFs inside or overlapping another ORF, not only the longest per region.
The genetic code for ORFfinder is derived from the curation ruleset.

In the Annotate details window, Auto-assign ORFs renames an ORF when it matches a protein-coding gene in the curation database. Delete ORFs that are not real genes before export.


Copy the gene from the reference (Liftover)
When a reference mitogenome contains a gene that is missing from your annotation, you can attempt to copy (liftover) the reference annotation. Liftover only copies annotations when the reference gene sequence is highly similar to an unannotated region of your sample’s assembly. Control regions and genes split into several pieces in the reference cannot be lifted over. See add a missing gene from the reference for the full walkthrough.

title: Difficult Annotations
section: Wrong strand, start position, or reading frame
text:
Wrong strand, start position, or reading frame
The whole assembly is backwards. MitoPilot orients each assembly from its rRNAs and starting gene. For taxa where that fails (for example, scyphozoan jellyfish with rRNAs on opposite strands) tick Reverse-complement assembly to match reference orientation. Each contig is then oriented to match the top BLAST reference.
A circular assembly starts in the wrong place. In the annotation options window, the Starting gene for circular assemblies sets the starting position for circular assemblies. If you wish to modify the start position of a single circular assembly after annotation, use the Rotate button in the Annotate details window. Picking a feature on the minus strand will also reverse-complements the assembly. Use the Restore assembly button to revert this change.
Genes have many internal stop codons or odd boundaries. Check the translation table first. In the Curation options, Genetic code is set from the curation ruleset unless you override it, so setting the wrong ruleset for your samples produces incorrect translations.

title: Difficult Annotations
section: The reference is a poor match
text:
The reference is a poor match
Two different references are in play, and they can be adjusted in different ways.
The BLAST reference is the closest GenBank mitogenome found for each assembly. The synteny viewer and Liftover use this reference. A distant or poorly annotated reference makes the synteny view misleading and gives Liftover little to copy.

Pick a better BLAST reference. In BLAST Reference Synteny, use the dropdown to view the other top BLAST hits, then Set … as best reference to keep one. This does not re-run curation, so existing validation warnings stay as they are.

The curation database is used to check gene boundaries. The warnings (low reference similarity, check reference start alignment, check reference stop alignment) utilize this database, not the best BLAST reference you set above.

Use a custom curation database. The bundled database contains RefSeq proteins. If your clade is poorly represented, build your own with custom_curation_db(). Then tick Use custom curation database in the Curation options, enter the location of your database, and re-run the annotation workflow. See building custom databases.

title: Difficult Annotations
text:
Fixing annotations by hand
Even with optimal annotation settings, manual review and edits are still often required. Use the Annotate details window to inspect the results and make these manual edits. The annotation walkthrough covers each tool in more detail. Briefly:

Move a start or stop codon. Select a protein-coding gene, open Alignment, and click Edit. The + and - buttons jump to the next valid start or stop codon while the alignment to the reference proteins updates.
Mark a gene partial. The Partial 5' and 3' buttons record an undetermined start or stop. Use them sparingly; GenBank may question a record with many partial genes.
Join a split gene. Merge PCGs/rRNAs joins pieces of one gene that were annotated separately.
Remove a false gene. Delete removes an annotation; Restore brings it back.

To discard all manual edits for an assembly and start again, set its state as Ready to run and update with the Nextflow -resume flag. See restoring annotations.
Validation warnings are not cleared when you fix the problem; they record the state when annotation workflow ran. Use the Reviewed button to track your progress.

title: Difficult Annotations
text:
A last check at export
Annotation boundary errors are easiest to spot by comparing across samples. When you export a group with Review PCG annotations for outliers ticked, MitoPilot aligns each protein-coding gene across the group and flags samples whose gene looks truncated, extended, or highly divergent from the rest. From the review window you can jump straight to the Annotate details window for a flagged sample. See the outlier review.

title: Choosing an Assembly Method
text:
MitoPilot can build a mitogenome from your reads in three ways. Two of them, GetOrganelle and MitoFinder, assemble the genome de novo from read overlaps, with no prior model of the sequence. The third, MapToRef, aligns the reads to a reference mitogenome you supply and builds a consensus sequence from the read pileup.
The method is chosen per sample in the Assembly Opts. window of the Assemble module, or for the whole project with the assembler argument of new_project(). Everything downstream (annotation, curation, export) works the same whichever you pick.

title: Choosing an Assembly Method
text:
At a glance










GetOrganelle (default)
MitoFinder
MapToRef




How it works
Recruits mitochondrial reads with seed sequences, then assembles them
Assembles all reads, then identifies mitochondrial contigs against a reference database
Aligns reads to one reference mitogenome, then calls a consensus from the pileup


Needs
Seed and label databases for your group (fish defaults ship with MitoPilot)
A GenBank file of reference mitogenomes for your group (fish defaults ship with MitoPilot)
One complete mitogenome per sample, from a close relative


Speed and memory
Fast, low memory
Slowest, highest memory
Fast, low memory


Output
One or more assembly paths, possibly split into scaffolds
One path, possibly several scaffolds
Always one path, one sequence


Best for
Most projects, especially clean whole-genome shotgun data
Groups with few reference mitogenomes, or when GetOrganelle fails to recruit reads
Low-coverage, short, or degraded reads; large batches of samples with a close reference


Watch out for
Depends on good seeds; tangled graphs yield several competing paths
Runtime; can recover NUMTs or contaminants
Cannot detect rearrangements or novel sequence; a distant reference gives a gappy, reference-biased consensus




Tip. Start with GetOrganelle. Switch to MitoFinder when GetOrganelle returns nothing or fragments, and you have a decent reference database for your group. Use MapToRef when you already have a mitogenome from the same or a very closely related species and your reads are low coverage, short, or damaged (e.g. ancient DNA), or when you want the fastest processing of many similar samples.

title: Choosing an Assembly Method
text:
GetOrganelle
GetOrganelle starts from a seed database of known mitochondrial sequences, recruits reads that match them, extends the assembly outward, and iterates until the genome closes. A label database of reference genes then identifies which parts of the assembly graph are mitochondrial. Because it only assembles the reads it recruits, it is fast and light on memory, but it is only as good as its seed database. You can build your own with custom_assembly_db() (see building custom databases).
The GetOrganelle options box carries the command-line flags. The defaults (-R 10, a k-mer series of 21 to 115, an expected genome size of 16.5 kb) work well for vertebrate mitogenomes. See the GetOrganelle wiki provides helpful guidance on the assembly parameters. For example, you can raise -R (the number of extension rounds) if assemblies are incomplete.
GetOrganelle is the only method that can return several assembly paths: alternative traversals of a tangled assembly graph, usually differing at a few sites. See handling difficult assemblies for how to resolve them.

title: Choosing an Assembly Method
text:
MitoFinder
MitoFinder assembles all reads with a general-purpose assembler, then searches the contigs for matches to a MitoFinder database, which is a GenBank-format file of one or more reference mitogenomes. Because reads are not filtered up front, it can recover mitogenomes that GetOrganelle’s seeds miss, at the cost of assembling everything. Expect much longer runtimes and higher memory use. Raise Memory in the Assembly options if samples fail with out-of-memory errors.
Two things to set:

MitoFinder database. The default is a small sampler of fish mitogenomes. For anything else, supply a .gb file of mitogenomes from your group, built with custom_assembly_db() or downloaded from GenBank. It only needs to be similar enough for MitoFinder to identify the mitochondrial contigs by sequence similarity.
MitoFinder options. MitoFinder can use three different assemblers. The default --megahit is the fastest; --metaspades is slower but often yields longer, more contiguous assemblies; --idba (IDBA-UD) is a third option. Any other MitoFinder flag can be added here too (see the MitoFinder documentation).

MitoFinder returns a single path. If it recovers more than one mitochondrial contig, they appear as separate scaffolds of that path. Inspect them in the assembly details window: fragments of one genome can be joined, while a NUMT or contaminant should be marked ignored.

title: Choosing an Assembly Method
text:
MapToRef
MapToRef is not actually an assembler. It aligns the reads to a reference mitogenome, calls a consensus sequence from the pileup, then uses that consensus as the reference for the next pass, iterating (up to Maximum passes, default 5) until the sequence converges. Use more iterations if your reference is a distant relative. The reference only determines where reads are placed; every base in the consensus comes from your reads. Sites with fewer than three reads are called N, and mixed sites get IUPAC ambiguity codes, which can trip annotation in coding regions, so check flagged sites before export.
This makes MapToRef the right tool when coverage is too low or reads too short or damaged for de novo assembly. MapToRef is the wrong tool when the sample may differ structurally from the reference: mapping cannot detect a gene rearrangement, a duplication, or sequence absent from the reference. If structure is uncertain, run a de novo assembly on a few samples and compare.
Reference. Set per sample rather than in the assembly options. One complete mitogenome given as a file path (GenBank .gb preferred, one record per file), a URL, or an NCBI accession such as NC_002333, through the mapping file’s Reference column, set_maptoref_refs(), or the sample’s MapToRef Ref cell in the Assemble table. A FASTA reference also needs its topology info (circular or linear). See starting your own project for the mapping-file format. The closer the reference the better: MitoPilot flags the result when more than 10% of called sites differ from the reference, and when more than half of the reference could not be called. If you change a sample’s reference after it has run, the sample is re-queued.
Mapper. Three choices in the Assembly options:

bowtie2 (default). Suits modern Illumina reads. Presets go in the options box: --very-sensitive-local is the default; add -N 1 for a more distant reference.
bwa-mem. Also suits modern reads, particularly longer ones. Leave the options empty for bwa’s defaults, or use -B 2 -T 20 (lower mismatch penalty, lower score threshold) for a distant reference.
bwa-aln. For short or damaged reads such as ancient DNA or degraded museum tissue. The default options (-l 1024 -n 0.01 -o 2) disable seeding and relax the edit distance, the standard ancient-DNA settings.

Whichever mapper you pick, the first pass against your reference runs with relaxed seeding so a distant reference still recruits reads; later passes use your options as given. The samtools consensus options box controls how the consensus is called from the pileup (default -d 3 --min-BQ 20: minimum depth 3, minimum base quality 20). A few flags are fixed by MitoPilot; adding one of them fails the sample with a message naming the flag.
Reading the result. A circular reference is mapped across its origin, but the assembly is only published as circular if reads span the junction; otherwise it is published as linear with a note saying so. The assembly details window for a MapToRef sample opens a sequence viewer. It shows read depth (zero-coverage positions highlighted red), the reference’s gene annotations, the reference and consensus sequences, and, below 1,000 bp of zoom, the individual reads with mismatches, indels, and strand. If you change a sample’s reference after it has run, the window flags the change and the sample is re-queued.

title: Choosing an Assembly Method
text:
Mixing methods in one project
Options are saved as named sets, and each sample points at one, so a project can use GetOrganelle for most samples and MitoFinder or MapToRef for the difficult ones. Make a second set in the Assembly options (tick Edit, change the assembler, give the set a new Parameter set name, click Save), then assign it to the samples that need it. The MapToRef reference is still set per sample. See the Assemble walkthrough for the options window.
